seo_desc: German settler folklore in Frederick County and the 1909 Maryland newspaper that invented sightings to sell copies. Then a museum and a beer festival.
summary: Maryland's beaked, tentacled dragon, a German settler story that a 1909 newspaper turned into a national sensation and then admitted was a stunt.
body: The snallygaster is Maryland's monster, a half-bird half-reptile thing with a metal beak full of teeth, claws like hooks and, in some tellings, octopus tentacles. The name comes from the German schneller Geist, or quick ghost, and it started with the German families who settled around Frederick County in the 1730s.

What made it famous was a newspaper. In February and March 1909 the Middletown Valley Register ran a series of sightings that went out on the wire and turned into a national story, complete with a Smithsonian reward and a president supposedly thinking about hunting it.
The sightings were made up by the paper's own editor and a reporter, to sell copies. That's the best part of the story and the part most retellings skip.

sections.h: A quick ghost from the German settlements
p: German immigrants settled the Frederick County area from the 1730s, and their hand-me-down monster was a schneller Geist, a quick ghost. Early versions were part bird like a siren and part demon, a thing that swooped out of the sky and carried off people and livestock, and some accounts had it drinking blood. The metal beak, the razor teeth and the tentacles got added over time, the way these things usually go.

The detail I like is the barns. Seven-pointed stars were painted on barns around there to keep the snallygaster away (seven, not five, and nobody seems to know why), and you can still find them on old buildings in the county. That's a folk remedy you can go and look at, which is more than most monster stories give you.

In February and March 1909 the Middletown Valley Register reported a beast with enormous wings, a long pointed bill, claws like steel hooks and a single eye in the middle of its forehead, screeching like a locomotive whistle (which is a specific and strange thing to compare a scream to). It was seen around South Mountain, Braddock Heights and the Middletown Valley, and then all over central Maryland, Berkeley County in West Virginia and the Washington area, because once a story like that gets on the wire it doesn't stay local.

The publicity got silly fast. The Smithsonian was said to be offering a reward for the hide, and Theodore Roosevelt reportedly thought about putting off an African safari to go and hunt the thing himself. Whether either of those is exactly true is hard to pin down, which is how tall tales work.

It was a stunt. The paper's editor, George C. Rhoderick, and a reporter, Ralph S. Wolfe, made the reports up to push circulation, and the creature they described borrowed from German folklore and from the [Jersey Devil](/creatures/jersey-devil/) reports that had run a few weeks earlier. A Maryland newspaper inventing a monster to sell papers, in the same winter another state's newspapers were doing the same thing with a devil, is a better story than the monster.

There's a darker layer under the snallygaster. Writers have speculated that the legend was kept alive in the 19th century to frighten freed African-Americans, and that fits the way these creatures got used around the region.

By the middle of the 20th century the word had turned into a general insult for a bogeyman. Whittaker Chambers used it in a 1953 Life essay to go after Senator Joseph McCarthy, calling him a national snallygaster and then explaining in brackets that he meant "a winged hobgoblin used to frighten naughty children in parts of rural Maryland". Marylanders were using the name for any scary nonsense long after the dragon had stopped appearing in papers.

For a hoax from 1909, the snallygaster has had a good run. J.K. Rowling put one in the 2017 edition of Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them as a relative of the Occamy. Fallout 76 has one, as a failed genetic experiment, which is a fair use of the name. There's a whiskey called Snallygaster from a distillery in Frederick (a blended one), a Snallygaster cafe in Harpers Ferry, and a beer festival in Washington DC that has been running since 2011 under the subtitle Beastly Beer Jamboree.

There's also an American Snallygaster Museum in Libertytown, Maryland, opened in 2021 by cryptozoologist Sarah Cooper, and a 2008 history of the legend by Patrick Boyton. For a creature that never existed, it has a museum, a whiskey and a festival, which is more than most real animals manage.

South Mountain and the Middletown Valley are the ground the 1909 stories came from, and it's good walking country with Civil War history all over it. Braddock Heights is where a lot of the sightings were placed, up on the ridge with the view the paper was selling.

Looking for seven-pointed stars on old barns is the honest version of monster hunting here. They exist, they were painted for exactly this reason (and they're easier to spot than a bird-reptile), and finding one beats standing in a field at midnight waiting for a bird-reptile that a newspaper editor made up in 1909.

faq.a: A monster from the folklore of German settlers in Frederick County, Maryland, described as half bird and half reptile with a metallic beak, sharp teeth, hooked claws and sometimes tentacles. The name comes from schneller Geist, meaning quick ghost, and seven-pointed stars painted on barns were meant to keep it away.

Frederick County, Maryland, particularly South Mountain, Braddock Heights and the Middletown Valley. The 1909 reports spread across central Maryland, Berkeley County in West Virginia and the Washington DC area. If you're asked this for school, the short answer is Maryland.

The 1909 sightings were. The Middletown Valley Register's editor George C. Rhoderick and reporter Ralph S. Wolfe invented them to boost circulation, borrowing details from German folklore and from the Jersey Devil stories printed weeks earlier. The older German settler folklore it grew out of is a separate thing.

Yes. The American Snallygaster Museum opened in Libertytown, Maryland in 2021, run by cryptozoologist Sarah Cooper. There's also a snallygaster beer festival in Washington DC every year and a whiskey of the same name from a Frederick distillery.

faq.q: Why did Teddy Roosevelt want to hunt the snallygaster?
faq.a: Newspapers in 1909 reported that he considered postponing an African safari to go after it. It came out of the same publicity wave the Middletown Valley Register was running, so treat it as part of the stunt rather than an actual presidential plan.
